consensus_summary: The blind responses converge on righteousness as right standing before God plus conformity to his character, with the dominant reading (especially Protestant) being God's righteousness imputed to believers through faith apart from works (Rom 3-4; 2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9), symbolized by a bestowed garment (Isa 61:10; Rev 19:8). Ethical/behavioral righteousness, infused righteousness, covenant faithfulness, and social justice appear as secondary or alternative senses, but the forensic-relational gift-by-faith core is treated as the primary meaning.
book_summary: The book defines righteousness as the actual doing of God's commandments — the law kept and worn as a garment of righteous acts — and explicitly denies that it is merely a received verdict or vague goodness, citing Deut 6:25, Ps 119:172, and 1 John 3:7. Its own common-view note acknowledges it is departing from the standard imputed-righteousness teaching.
rationale: The book does not merely emphasize the ethical strand (which the consensus lists as a 'common' alternative); it elevates commandment-keeping to the primary definition while expressly negating the consensus's dominant sense ('not... a verdict only received'). Because it displaces rather than sharpens the recognizable primary meaning — imputed/forensic right standing received by faith — this is DIVERGENT, not REFINED. The book's inclusion of a common-view note contrasting itself with imputed righteousness confirms it understands itself as contradicting the mainstream reading.
strongest_objection: Ethical/behavioral righteousness is already a recognized 'common' alternative in all three blind responses (Matt 5:20; 1 John 3:7; Ezek 18), so one could argue the book merely promotes an existing minority-within-consensus reading and should be classed REFINED. Additionally, the printed citations, while directly equating righteousness with doing commandments, do not engage the Pauline texts (Rom 4:3-8; Phil 3:9) that ground the view the book rejects, so its negative claim ('not a verdict only received') rests on omission rather than direct rebuttal.
